Captain Noel Godfrey Chavasse was the Victoria Cross recipient who served in the greatest number of conflicts: awarded the VC twice in World War I, and also served in the Balkan Wars and the Palestine Campaign. #chavasse #victoria-cross
Chavasse's first Victoria Cross was for tending and rescuing wounded soldiers under heavy fire at the Battle of Guillemont during the 1916 Somme offensive. #chavasse #victoria-cross

Chavasse's second Victoria Cross was for continuing to tend wounded soldiers under heavy enemy fire at the Battle of Passchendaele in 1917; he died of his wounds in the Ypres Salient in 1917 and was posthumously awarded the Military Cross. #chavasse #victoria-cross
Chavasse was born in Oxford in 1884, son of Francis James Chavasse, a Church of England bishop, and his wife Edith, a nurse; he had six siblings, four brothers and two sisters. #chavasse

Chavasse was educated at Oxford University, where he was a distinguished sportsman, then studied medicine at Liverpool University, graduating in 1906; he worked as a doctor in Liverpool before joining the Royal Army Medical Corps in 1913. #chavasse
Chavasse married his wife Gladys in 1915 and they had one daughter, also named Gladys; he was a deeply religious man known for his faith and dedication to his patients. #chavasse

A statue of Chavasse was erected in Liverpool in 1919 in the gardens of the Liverpool Anglican Cathedral, sculpted by Francis Derwent Wood; it shows him in army uniform holding a medical bag and is a realistic likeness. #chavasse #liverpool

In the Balkan Wars (1912-1913) Chavasse served with a British medical mission in Serbia, caring for wounded soldiers of both sides; in the Palestine Campaign (from late 1916) he was a medical officer, including at the Battle of Gaza in 1917. #chavasse

Chavasse's medal collection, including his two Victoria Crosses, is held at the Imperial War Museum in London; he was commemorated in Liverpool, where he is regarded as a famous son. #chavasse #victoria-cross

Artwork notes discussed 2023-03-19: Francisco de Goya's etching "Y no hai remedio (And There's Nothing to Be Done)" from the series Los Desastres de la Guerra (The Disasters of War), made c. 1810-1820 during the Peninsular War. Content: a bound victim about to be shot, depicting death, destruction and civilian suffering. Function: anti-war political/social commentary and warning about war's horrors. #art #Goya #DisastersOfWar

Artwork notes discussed 2023-03-19: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, "La Grande Odalisque", 1814, a prime example of French Neoclassicism (with Romantic/orientalist touches). Content: a reclining nude odalisque with exotic turban, peacock-feather fan and jewelry on a couch, famous for her elongated back. Function: idealized female form offered as an object of beauty/desire, reflecting European bourgeois fascination with the exotic Orient. #art #Ingres #Neoclassicism

Artwork notes discussed 2023-03-19: Eugène Delacroix, "Liberty Leading the People", 1830, a landmark of French Romanticism commemorating the July Revolution of 1830. Content: the allegorical figure of Liberty holding the Tricolor and a musket, leading soldiers and civilians over fallen bodies. Function: celebration of revolutionary ideals (liberty, equality, fraternity) and a political call to action; an icon of French national identity. #art #Delacroix #Romanticism

Artwork notes discussed 2023-03-19: Thomas Cole, "The Oxbow (View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm)", 1836, a masterpiece of the Hudson River School. Content: panoramic view of the Connecticut River's oxbow bend, wilderness and storm at left, cultivated farmland and a tiny self-portrait at right. Function: celebration of American landscape and national identity, and a meditation on wilderness versus civilization/progress. #art #ThomasCole #HudsonRiverSchool

Artwork notes discussed 2023-03-19: J.M.W. Turner, "Slave Ship (Slavers Throwing Overboard the Dead and Dying, Typhoon Coming On)", exhibited 1840 at the Royal Academy. Content: a slave ship in a typhoon, crew throwing dead and dying enslaved people overboard; gory detail in the foreground sea, blazing sunset. Function: condemnation of the transatlantic slave trade, evoking shock, horror and empathy; also a demonstration of Turner's mastery of light and colour. #art #Turner #Romanticism

Artwork notes discussed 2023-03-19: Palace of Westminster (Houses of Parliament), London — Gothic Revival complex rebuilt after the 1834 fire, designed by Charles Barry with Augustus Pugin, main structure dating from the mid-to-late 19th century. Houses the House of Commons and House of Lords; includes the Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben). Functions as seat of British government, symbol of British democracy, and major tourist landmark. #art #architecture #London

Artwork notes discussed 2023-03-19: Gustave Courbet, "The Stone Breakers", 1849 (an important work of 19th-century Realism). Content: an old, frail man and a young boy breaking stones in a barren landscape, their faces hidden. Function: unromanticized social commentary on labour and poverty under the Industrial Revolution, a critique of inequality and a call for social justice; the original was destroyed in 1945. #art #Courbet #Realism

Artwork notes discussed 2023-03-19: Eadweard Muybridge, "Horse in Motion" (1878) — a series of photographs of a galloping horse taken with multiple tripwire-triggered cameras, commissioned by Leland Stanford to settle whether a horse ever has all four hooves off the ground. A foundational work of motion photography and a precursor to motion pictures, used by artists and animators to study movement. #art #Muybridge #photography
